title: Story ideas for when you're out of inspiration
meta_description: Ready-made story ideas for days when your imagination has run dry. Faceless, wordless formats that take almost no effort.
og_description: What to post to stories when your head is empty but you still want to publish every day.

blocks.text: The main mistake is treating a story like a scaled-down post: same prep, same lighting, same copy. Then every story turns into a project you don't feel like spending energy on when you're having a rough day.
A story is a draft, a report from the scene. The less polished it is, the more often it gets a response - because it looks like a normal message from a friend, not an ad.

sections.h2: Ideas with no face and no words

items: A cup of tea or coffee in close-up with a single mood caption
The view from your window right now, just as it is
Hands doing an ordinary task - cooking, laundry, playing with your kid
Your phone screen with the playlist that's on right now
The mess on your desk as-is, with no tidying up for the camera
One object of the day - the thing that saved you today

sections.h2: Ideas with a question to your followers

blocks.text: Questions work because they take the burden of coming up with content off you - the content comes from the answers in comments and reactions.

items: What to cook for dinner - give two options to choose from
Who's also having a hard day - tag it with a reaction
Which piece of advice from the blog actually came in handy
What to read tonight - suggest a book in reply
Did you have a similar situation this week

sections.h2: Ideas from what you've already shot

blocks.text: Not everything has to be new. Your gallery already holds a week's worth of material, if you see it not as an archive but as a reserve.

items: A shot from a walk this week with a new caption
A screenshot of an old post marked "still relevant"
A photo from a year ago with a note on what has changed
A clip that didn't make it into the main post

blocks.text: Your followers don't remember your stories by heart. What feels like a repeat to you is a first time for them.

sections.h2: Ideas for days with a little more energy

blocks.text: Sometimes you have energy for more than a photo - for something a bit more developed. Then reach for formats that still shoot without prep or rehearsals.

items: A short voice-over on a video with the thought that circled in your head all day
A breakdown of one question from the comments over the past week
Before and after - any small thing that changed at home or in you
A three-point list on a topical subject with no long explanations

blocks.text: These formats don't replace a full post, but they keep contact with your followers on the days between posts - and that's part of the blog too, not a pause in it.

sections.h2: How much effort each format takes

blocks.text: On a low-energy day, one format from the left column is enough. You don't need to fill every slot at once - one story today beats none at all. Over time you'll notice which formats come easiest to you, and you'll return to them automatically, without overthinking.

faq.q: How many stories should I post per day?
faq.a: One or two is enough. Consistency matters more than the count on any single day.

faq.q: What do I do if I have no ideas at all today?
faq.a: Take any idea from the section on what you've already shot - it's the fastest option with no new filming.

faq.q: Do I have to speak on camera in stories?
faq.a: No. Faceless, voiceless formats work just as well and suit the days when you don't feel like being on camera.

faq.q: How do I tell which stories land better?
faq.a: Look at replies and reactions, not just views. Questions almost always get more response than a monologue.

faq.q: Do I need to prepare stories in advance?
faq.a: Not necessarily. Some ideas from this list can be shot and published in a minute, right now.
